entry_state: The actual option settles once, whereas the hypothetical option measures the hedged risk. A fully aligned zero-cost collar can reverse both signed reserves without becoming a general unmatched allocation rule. Rebalancing retains item-layer origins and instrument acquisition values; only subsequent designated gains enter the cumulative hedge. Reducing half of instrument A leaves its earlier gains intact and the purchase volume unchanged; the general removal-history notation has just begun.
exit_state: Instrument reduction freezes earlier designated gains without removing purchase volume. Stopping a homogeneous purchase portion instead freezes its attached reserve, with expectation and loss findings deciding later release. Distinct perfectly matched designation origins give different canceled-purchase outcomes even with identical derivative cash. Inventory receipt then transfers the retained reserve to cost directly; terminal totals alone can conceal a wrong interim profit entry.

findings.judgment: The G/U decomposition retains values at each removal date and adds back to each actual instrument value. Removing B rather than A keeps the same remaining nominal amount but yields reserve 200 instead of 190 and profit 20 instead of 30. Settlement and inventory cash bridges make the economically different histories visible without presenting nominal fractions as valuations.

The proportional split is derived only for identical per-unit exposures and one common origin. The stopped derivative value 240 and reserve 200 are distinct origins; later 40 gains enter earnings while the reserve stays frozen. No-longer-expected and unrecoverable-loss cases release only amounts still attached, avoiding both continued hedging of stopped volume and double-counted loss releases.

The 15-versus-10 stopped gain counterexample motivates named designation origins before q, date and price notation. Same-sign exact offsets derive the relationship-level lower-of result; a sum of independent minima is explicitly not substituted. The split identity preserves frozen gain, continuing reserve and post-cessation gain, with signed releases reconciling D = Rc + F + P.

Canceled A/B histories have the same 70 derivative receipt and 190 cash but different inventory and profit. Expected purchases can share terminal totals while still needing their different reserve origins. Loss release cannot be restored by a later instrument rise. The 240-versus-239 payment-order example explains intermediate funding refusal; matched origins and one stop remain explicit finite-method limits.

The inventory transfer is motivated as the end of the reserve's deferral, with gain and loss cases reversing directions consistently. K = C - R and the later profit cancellation distinguish basis adjustment from earnings and cash. The final counterexample shows how an incorrect immediate profit credit could disappear in terminal totals, so matching the closing book is not treated as sufficient validation.
